newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African T-Bill rate seen dipping again on Friday.
newsitem.headline: S.African T-Bill rate seen dipping again on Friday.

text.p: The Reserve Bank kept its weekly offer of 91-day Treasury Bills at 600 million rand on Thursday, prompting dealers to predict yet another fall in the average rate.
Dealers said the lower offer, which up until three weeks ago was regularly pegged at 900 million rand, indicated the rate could fall to between 15.60 and 15.70 percent from 15.79 percent last week.

A central bank money market official, who declined to be identified, said the lower offer -- set in conjunction with the Finance Department -- was a result of government's August funding programme "going a little bit better than planned".
"We simply reduced it because of the fact that the government's finance situation was a little bit better in August than it should have been," the spokesman said.
He agreed with market views that the reduced offer was a bid to reduce the speculative element at the weekly tender.

"By reducing the tender they take out all the guys who scalp it at the top," one trader said of players who tendered very high in a bid to push up the rate and end up with "a good asset on their books".
"What we saw after reducing the offer was a lot more serious tendering...the speculative element was limited," the spokesman said.
One trader noted that although the rate was expected to be lower, it was unlikely to be low enough to justify the current levels of three-month NCD rates.
"In terms of where the 3-month NCDs are trading at the moment, the tender should come out at 15.35 percent," he said.
Various banks were quoting NCDs at between 15.90 and 16.05 percent on Thursday.
"My perception is that it is going to come out about the 15.60 levels, in other words lower, but not low enough to justify where the three-month NCDs are.
"If it comes out at 15.60 percent it implies a yield on the NCDs of 16.25, in which case the NCDs will go up...they will have to reset themselves," he said.
Dealers noted that the bank had also kept its offer for 182 day bills at 200 million rand for the second successive week, compared with the regular 100 million.
"Logic would say that they expect rates to go up because they are funding more longer," a senior trader said.
The bank official said the higher offer of six-month bills was a result of the central bank "noticing that there was a lot more interest from the market in the six-month area".
The results of the tender will be announced at 1000 GMT on Friday.
Traders said that contrary to expectations last week, the market shortage had shown no noticeable signs of easing.
The bank spokesman that initial indications were that the shortage would remain around the eight billion rand mark going into next week, but that this could change after about two-weeks.

"The estimates that we have at this stage indicate that there is still a marginal outflow of capital out of the country. As long as that is taking place then I don't think that we will see the shortage coming below eight billion," he said.
The bank quoted the shortage at 8.532 billion rand on Wednesday from 8.551 billion rand on Tuesday.
-- Johannesburg newsroom, +27 11 482-1003
